routes.description: Establish God through convergent natural-theology inferences from actualized change, intelligible natural order, objective morality, and interpersonal knowledge.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if these features require a transcendent actual source, ordering intellect, and ground of moral obligation properly identifiable as God.

motionBridge.description: Connect the inferred first cause, ordering mind, and moral ground to the God affirmed by Thomistic theism.

centralBridges.description: Show that dependent change and instrumental causal series require a purely actual first source.
Show that reliable natural regularity and intelligibility require an ordering intellect beyond mindless objects.
Show that obligations independent of human opinion require grounding in a divine intellect.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend natural theology as legitimate inference from observed effects to an explanatory cause.
Explain how interpersonal knowledge could warrant belief in God beyond scientific testing alone.

routes.description: Withhold belief unless the affirmative defines God and supplies supported inferences that establish divine attributes rather than merely an unexplained cause.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the proposed proofs leave unsupported causal, methodological, moral, or revelatory gaps, making nonbelief the warranted tentative position.

motionBridge.description: Show that the affirmative evidence does not warrant the conclusion that the claimed God exists.

centralBridges.description: Require a defined claim and valid, evidentially supported demonstration from the side asserting God.
Separate any inferred cause or regularity from the divine mind and maximal attributes claimed.
Account for objective moral assessment relative to human well-being without positing divine moral law.
Require adequate detectable disclosure from a capable personal God who wants to be known.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Limit explanatory candidates to causes that have been independently shown to be demonstrable.
Maintain the negative conclusion tentatively and permit revision upon a sound supported demonstration.

sectionSelections.title: Burden of proof and warranted belief
sectionSelections.rationale: The governing evidential standard determines what the affirmative must establish and when skeptical nonbelief remains warranted.

proSelections.proposition: Chains of potency, causation, and contingency require an actual and necessary source beyond dependent natural chains, identified as God.

conSelections.proposition: The party asserting God bears the burden, and inability to disprove an undefined or unfalsifiable God does not justify belief.
Belief should remain revisable because no adequate definition, physical support, or valid and sound evidence-backed argument for God has been supplied.

sectionSelections.title: Change, causation, and the first mover
sectionSelections.rationale: The causal inference and the identification of its terminus are indispensable steps in the principal Thomistic route to the motion.

proSelections.proposition: Change from potency to actuality through an instrumental causal series that cannot regress infinitely requires a purely actual first mover.
Thomistic causation may be simultaneous rather than temporally successive, while an infinite series of mere potencies cannot actualize change.

conSelections.proposition: Observed causal regularities within the accessible universe do not demonstrate causal extension beyond its history or coherent existence outside time.
A first-cause model does not establish that its cause is God or a mind, and atemporal causation has not been coherently demonstrated.

sectionSelections.title: Natural theology and scientific explanation
sectionSelections.rationale: Whether observations can support extranatural explanatory candidates controls the methodological standing of the affirmative natural-theology inferences.

proSelections.proposition: Reliable goal-directed behavior by mindless natural objects implies an intelligent mind guiding natural laws and regularities.
Natural observations can scientifically point toward an extranatural creator, first cause, necessary being, or intelligent designer.

conSelections.proposition: Scientific explanation may use demonstrable natural causes but cannot invoke undetectable supernatural entities without first establishing their detectability.

sectionSelections.title: Objective morality and divine grounding
sectionSelections.rationale: The existence, meaning, and possible grounding of objective moral judgment form an independent affirmative proof and a central secular alternative.

proSelections.proposition: Objective moral obligations beyond individual opinion require a divine intellect in which moral law is grounded.
Reducing morality to evolved human preference makes condemnation of even extreme wrongdoing merely a matter of opinion.

conSelections.proposition: Once morality is grounded in the well-being of thinking creatures, objective physical facts permit assessments without universal divine law.
Invoking God does not resolve competing moral codes, while secular systems can pursue workable consensus through discussion, evidence, and debate.

sectionSelections.title: Divine hiddenness and interpersonal knowledge
sectionSelections.rationale: A personal God's manner of disclosure bears directly on whether private knowledge can answer the demand for publicly adequate evidence.

proSelections.proposition: Knowledge of a personal God can transcend scientific proof, as people may directly know love in close relationships without scientifically demonstrating it.

conSelections.proposition: A capable God who wants belief should provide detectable evidence, yet alleged revelations remain unverifiable or insufficient.
Private relationship claims and assertions about natural theology or morality do not demonstrate God's existence or answer divine hiddenness.
